AbnormalCase.description:
Abnormal Security case event, imported by Ingext from the Abnormal Security Cases API / event stream (the Account Takeover Protection / Email Security case feed). A case is Abnormal's correlated account-compromise (ATO) investigation: one potentially-compromised entity (usually a user account), the trigger that opened the case, a severity/confidence verdict, the human-readable insights and GenAI summary explaining why, and an event_timeline of the underlying sign-in / risk events that fed the case.
The record is wrapped in an envelope with two top-level objects:

  - abx_metadata — delivery metadata: event_type ("CASE"), the emit timestamp,
    and a trace_id.
  - abx_body — the case itself: identity (case_id, customer, tenant, entity),
    the verdict (severity, confidence, case_status, remediation_status,
    trigger_event), the explanation arrays (insights[], genai_summary[]), and
    the event_timeline[] of underlying events.

The event is stored as a dynamic JSON document, so reach into the envelope with dot notation (abx_body.case_id, abx_body.entity.identifier, abx_metadata.trace_id) and cast with tostring()/toint()/todatetime(). The arrays (abx_body.insights, abx_body.genai_summary, abx_body.event_timeline, abx_body.platforms) require mv-expand to enumerate. timestamp is parsed from abx_metadata.timestamp. Distinguish this stream from AbnormalThreat (email threats) by abx_metadata.event_type == "CASE".

AbnormalThreat.description:
Abnormal Security threat event, imported by Ingext from the Abnormal Security Threats API (the /threats and /threats/{threatId} endpoints of the Email Security / Inbound Email Security product). Each record is one detected threat campaign identified by threatId. A threat is a group of one or more related malicious messages (the same attack delivered to one or more recipients across the tenant), so the message-level detail lives in a 'messages' array — one element per delivered/detected email in the campaign.
Top level carries only the campaign identity and time (threatId, timestamp) plus the messages[] array; everything security-analysts care about (sender, recipient, subject, attack classification, remediation status, links, attachments, IPs) is per-message inside messages[]. The record is stored as a dynamic JSON document, so the messages array must be enumerated with mv-expand (or mv-apply) and its fields reached with dot notation on the expanded row (e.g. mv-expand messages | extend fromAddr = tostring(messages.fromAddress)). A single-message threat is the common case, but never assume length 1 — always mv-expand rather than indexing messages[0].
timestamp is parsed from the top-level 'timestamp'. Note that threatId appears both at the top level and on every message element (they match — the message's parent campaign).

CloudTrail.description:
AWS CloudTrail audit events, imported by Ingext from a CloudTrail trail (S3/CloudWatch Logs) or the CloudTrail Lake/event data store. Each record is one API-level activity event in an AWS account: who did what (userIdentity), which operation (eventName) on which service (eventSource), from where (sourceIPAddress, userAgent), when (eventTime), and the outcome (responseElements / errorCode).
Events fall into four categories (eventCategory):

  - Management — control-plane API calls (create/modify/delete/describe of AWS
    resources, IAM, console sign-in). The bulk of a trail. managementEvent = true.
  - Data — high-volume object-level operations on the resources themselves
    (S3 GetObject/PutObject, Lambda Invoke, DynamoDB item ops). eventCategory =
    "Data"; the resource is in resources[] / requestParameters.
  - Network — VPC endpoint activity (traffic reaching a service through a VPC
    endpoint), eventCategory = "NetworkActivity".
  - Insights — CloudTrail Insights anomaly-detection events, emitted when the rate
    of a management API call deviates from the learned baseline. eventCategory =
    "Insight"; carries an insightDetails object instead of a normal actor call.

Events also carry an eventType: AwsApiCall (a normal SDK/CLI/API call), AwsConsoleSignIn (console login, eventName ConsoleLogin), AwsServiceEvent (an action AWS itself performed, no external caller — detail in serviceEventDetails), AwsConsoleAction, AwsCloudTrailInsight, etc.
The event is stored as a dynamic JSON document, so nested fields use dot notation (e.g. userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName) and arrays (resources) require mv-expand to enumerate. requestParameters and responseElements are SERVICE-SPECIFIC — their shape depends on eventSource and eventName, so treat them as free-form dynamic objects and reach in with tostring(requestParameters.<field>). Both are frequently null. timestamp is parsed from eventTime.
userIdentity is a complex, polymorphic object whose shape depends on userIdentity.type — IAMUser, Root, AssumedRole, AWSService, AWSAccount, FederatedUser, IdentityCenterUser (SSO), WebIdentityUser, Directory, etc. See the userIdentity field notes below for how to resolve the acting principal across these variants (the sessionContext.sessionIssuer sub-object is the key to getting the underlying role/user behind an AssumedRole).

CortexAlert.description: PaloAlto Cortex XDR alert, imported by Ingext from the Cortex XDR API (Get Alerts / alerts endpoint). Each record is one detection raised by a Cortex detector (XDR Agent local analysis, BIOC, correlation, firewall, etc.) on one endpoint: the alert identity and classification, the affected agent/host, the triggering rule, resolution/matching status, and a nested 'events' array holding the raw causality-graph event(s) that produced the alert (actor/causality/OS process lineage, file/registry/network actions, and firewall fields). Alerts are grouped into a CortexIncident via case_id (= the incident's incident_id). The object is stored as a dynamic JSON document, so nested fields use dot notation (e.g. events[0].actor_process_image_name) and the 'events' array requires mv-expand to enumerate. timestamp is parsed from detection_timestamp.

CortexIncident.description: PaloAlto Cortex XDR incident, imported by Ingext from the Cortex XDR API (Get Incidents / incidents endpoint). It carries the incident identity and status, severity (effective and the per-severity alert counts), the aggregated/predicted/manual risk scores, the affected hosts and users, the contributing alert categories and sources, MITRE mapping, assignment/resolution metadata, and a deep link to the Cortex console. Alerts join to their incident via CortexAlert.case_id == incident_id. The object is stored as a dynamic JSON document, so array fields (hosts, users, alert_categories, incident_sources) require mv-expand. timestamp is parsed from creation_time.

DuoAdmin.description:
Cisco Duo administrator log event, imported by Ingext from the Duo Admin API administrator logs (/admin/v1/logs/administrator). One record per administrative change made in the Duo Admin Panel or via the Admin API: who made the change (username), what they did (action), what it was applied to (object), and the change detail (description / descriptionFields).
This is the audit stream for the MFA control plane itself. High-value actions to watch: bypass-code creation (bypass_create), user/phone re-enrollment or reactivation (user_update, phone_update, user_reset_activation), policy and integration edits (policy_update, integration_update, integration_delete), and admin-account changes (admin_create, admin_update, admin_2fa_error/admin_login_error). A directory sync also writes here (ad_sync_finish and friends) under a synthetic service username.
Note the two representations of the same change detail: description is the raw JSON *string* Duo emits (use parse_json() to work with it), while descriptionFields is the same content already parsed into a dynamic object — prefer descriptionFields and reach in with dot notation. Its keys vary by action, and human-readable keys contain spaces, so index them with bracket syntax: descriptionFields["Users added"]. timestamp is parsed from isotimestamp. MFA login attempts are a separate stream — see DuoAuthentication.

DuoAuthentication.description:
Cisco Duo authentication log event, imported by Ingext from the Duo Admin API v2 authentication logs (/admin/v2/logs/authentication). One record per multi-factor authentication attempt: who authenticated (user), to what (application), from where (access_device — the endpoint originating the login), with which second factor (auth_device — the phone/token that approved it), and the outcome (result / reason / factor).
This is the primary MFA telemetry stream for detecting push fatigue / MFA bombardment (repeated result == "denied" with reason == "user_mistake" or "user_marked_fraud"), impossible-travel logins (access_device.location vs auth_device.location), policy bypass (factor == "bypass_code" or "remembered_device"), and out-of-date/untrusted endpoints (ood_software, trusted_endpoint_status).
Nested objects (user, application, access_device, auth_device, adaptive_trust_assessments) are stored as dynamic JSON — reach in with dot notation and cast with tostring()/toint()/tobool(); mv-expand user.groups to enumerate group membership. timestamp is parsed from isotimestamp (the epoch-second timestamp field carries the same instant). Administrative changes in Duo are a separate stream — see DuoAdmin.

FalconAlert.description:
CrowdStrike Falcon EDR alert, imported by Ingext from the Falcon Alerts API (the unified /alerts detections endpoint). Each record is one alert on one endpoint (agent_id / device). Alerts come in two shapes, distinguished by the 'type' field:

  - type = "automated-lead" (product "automated-lead"): the AI-generated
    summary/lead. Falcon's automated triage correlates related detections on a
    host into a single lead. These records are sparse on process detail but
    carry the rollup fields — score, aggregated mitre_attack[], the
    threatgraph_indicators[] array that lists the supporting indicators, and
    signal_start/end/updated timestamps spanning the correlated activity.
    lead_id / id identify the lead.

  - type = "signal" (product "automated-lead-context"): a supporting /
    contextual alert (one underlying detection) that rolls up into a lead. It
    is linked to its lead via aggregate_id = lead_id and carries the full
    detection detail: triggering process (cmdline / filename / filepath / md5
    / sha256), parent_details and grandparent_details process lineage, MITRE
    tactic/technique, pattern_disposition (whether it was blocked/prevented),
    prevention policy, the affected host 'device' object, and behavioral
    context arrays (dns_requests[], files_accessed[], files_written[],
    network_accesses[]).

Join a lead to its signals on FalconAlert(type="automated-lead").lead_id == FalconAlert(type="signal").aggregate_id. The object is stored as a dynamic JSON document, so nested fields use dot notation (e.g. device.hostname, parent_details.filename) and the arrays (mitre_attack, threatgraph_indicators, dns_requests, files_written, files_accessed, network_accesses) require mv-expand to enumerate. timestamp is parsed from the top-level 'timestamp' field (crawl/emit time). Many fields are null on one type or the other.

MSDefenderAlert.description:
Microsoft Defender XDR alert, imported by Ingext from the Microsoft Graph security API (GET /security/alerts_v2). Each record is one alert as surfaced in the Microsoft Defender portal (security.microsoft.com), regardless of which Microsoft security product raised it — Defender for Endpoint, Defender Antivirus, Defender for Office 365, Defender for Cloud Apps, Defender for Identity, Entra ID Protection, Defender for Cloud, Microsoft Sentinel analytic rules, Purview Insider Risk Management, and app-governance. The alert carries its classification (severity, category, MITRE techniques), the product and detector that produced it, the analyst workflow state (status, classification, determination, assignedTo, comments), and an evidence[] array of the entities involved (users, devices, processes, files, IPs, mailboxes, cloud apps, ...).
Every alert belongs to an incident: incidentId is the join key to MSDefenderIncident.id, and one incident typically groups several alerts from different serviceSources telling one story.
Two fields govern how to read the rest of the record:

  - serviceSource / detectionSource — which product raised the alert. This
    selects which evidence @odata.types appear and what additionalData holds.
    Note that products onboarded through the unified portal (Sentinel analytic
    rules, Purview IRM) report serviceSource == "unknownFutureValue" and
    detectionSource == "unknownFutureValue"; use productName to identify them.
  - evidence[].@odata.type — the entity kind of each evidence element. The
    array is heterogeneous, so always filter on @odata.type before reaching
    into type-specific fields.

The record is stored as a dynamic JSON document, so nested fields use dot notation (e.g. tostring(evidence[0].userAccount.userPrincipalName)) and the arrays (evidence, categories, mitreTechniques, comments, systemTags) require mv-expand / mv-apply to enumerate. Because '@odata.type' contains an @ and a dot, index it as a bracketed key: ev['@odata.type']. timestamp is parsed from createdDateTime. This stream is selected by the label eventType == "MSDefenderAlert".
Alerts are re-emitted as their state changes (status, classification, determination, assignedTo, comments, added evidence), so the same id appears more than once in a time range and must be reduced to its latest snapshot before counting, filtering on status, or reporting. This is observed, not theoretical: the two records in eventSamples/msDefenderAlert_defenderForOffice365_reemitted .json share id 'fa...ca' and are byte-identical except for lastUpdateDateTime (04:01:27.07 vs 04:02:21.846) — same status, same evidence, no new information in the second copy. Duplicates therefore inflate count() and any per-alert metric while adding nothing, and the interval between copies can be under a minute. Prefer dcount(id) over count() wherever a stray duplicate would distort a number.
IMPORTANT — this engine does not support arg_max(<column>, *) (the '*' cannot be expanded against a dynamic schema), so the usual Kusto one-liner is unavailable. Take the max lastUpdateDateTime per id and join it back instead; naming the key column on the right-hand side avoids relying on how the engine renames a duplicate join key:

  let LatestAlert =
      MSDefenderAlert
      | where timestamp > ago(7d)
      | summarize LastUpdate = max(todatetime(lastUpdateDateTime)) by AlertId = id;
  MSDefenderAlert
  | where timestamp > ago(7d)
  | join kind=inner LatestAlert on $left.id == $right.AlertId
  | where todatetime(lastUpdateDateTime) == LastUpdate
  | project-away AlertId, LastUpdate

Keep the two time windows identical, or the join will drop or resurrect rows. If two snapshots of one id ever share the same lastUpdateDateTime, both survive this pattern — arg_max would have picked exactly one — but they are duplicates of the same state, so it matters only for count() and dcount(id) is safer either way. Every query sample in queries/ opens with this block.
Should wildcard arg_max support be added for this case, the block collapses to 'summarize arg_max(lastUpdateDateTime, *) by id' with no other change to any query. queries/msd-alert-device-evidence-argmax.yaml holds that form side by side with the portable msd-alert-device-evidence.yaml — the two are identical from the first pipeline stage onward, so they double as the migration diff. It is tagged 'requires-wildcard-argmax' and must not be run until the engine supports it.

MSDefenderIncident.description:
Microsoft Defender XDR incident, imported by Ingext from the Microsoft Graph security API (GET /security/incidents). An incident is Defender's correlation container: the set of alerts — across Defender for Endpoint, Office 365, Cloud Apps, Identity, Entra ID Protection, Sentinel analytic rules, Insider Risk and Defender for Cloud — that Defender believes belong to one attack story, plus the workflow state for that story (severity, status, priority score, classification, determination, owner, comments, tags).
This is a small, flat record — there are no nested objects and no evidence. It answers "what is open, how bad is it, who owns it"; everything about *what happened* lives in MSDefenderAlert. Join them on MSDefenderIncident.id == MSDefenderAlert.incidentId. Note the incident document as ingested does NOT carry an alerts[] array (the connector does not request $expand=alerts), so the join is always required — see the query samples.
Three things about this stream will produce wrong answers if ignored:

  1. It is append-only snapshots, not current state. Every change to an
     incident emits another record with the same id: incident 101195 in the
     samples appears twice, first at creation (displayName "'TurtlePerlsh'
     high-severity malware was prevented", status active, priorityScore 24) and
     again after auto-resolution (displayName "Malware incident on one
     endpoint", status resolved, priorityScore 33). Always reduce to the latest
     snapshot before counting, filtering on status, or reporting. Both snapshots
     share the same createdDateTime — and therefore the same 'timestamp' — so
     ordering or de-duplicating by timestamp does not work; lastUpdateDateTime is
     the only field that distinguishes them.

     This engine does not support arg_max(<column>, *), because '*' cannot be
     expanded against a dynamic schema. Take the max per id and join it back:

       let LatestIncident =
           MSDefenderIncident
           | where timestamp > ago(30d)
           | summarize LastUpdate = max(todatetime(lastUpdateDateTime)) by IncId = id;
       MSDefenderIncident
       | where timestamp > ago(30d)
       | join kind=inner LatestIncident on $left.id == $right.IncId
       | where todatetime(lastUpdateDateTime) == LastUpdate
       | project-away IncId, LastUpdate

     Naming the right-hand key (IncId) avoids depending on how the engine renames
     a duplicated join key, and the two time windows must match. Every query
     sample in queries/ opens with this block — except msd-incident-history.yaml,
     which keeps the snapshots on purpose.

  2. displayName is not stable. Defender seeds it from the first alert's title
     and renames the incident as alerts are correlated in ("Malware incident on
     one endpoint", "Persistence incident involving multiple users"). Group by
     id, never by displayName. Titles also contain characters that break naive
     matching — one sample title carries a zero-width space (U+200B) inside
     "delivery​ involving" — so prefer 'contains'/'matches regex' on a
     leading substring over equality.

  3. classification and determination are the literal string "unknown" when
     untriaged, not null (unlike MSDefenderAlert, where they are null). A filter
     like 'where isnotempty(classification)' therefore matches every record;
     use 'where classification !in ("unknown", "")' instead.

Stored as a dynamic JSON document; the arrays (comments, customTags, systemTags) are dynamic and need mv-expand / array_length. timestamp is parsed from createdDateTime. This stream is selected by the label eventType == "MSDefenderIncident".

SentinelOneActivity.description: SentinelOne activity/audit event collected by Ingext from the SentinelOne management API (activities feed). Unlike the agent/application/threat resource snapshots, this is an append-only event stream: each record is one thing that happened in the console or on an endpoint — a login, a policy or config change, an agent action, a threat lifecycle transition, a Deep Visibility / STAR event, or a maintenance action such as merging Live Updates. The event kind is a numeric code in activityType, with human-readable text in primaryDescription / secondaryDescription and a per-type 'data' object holding the templated details. Site/group/account scope is denormalized onto each record. The object is stored as a dynamic JSON document, so nested fields use dot notation (e.g. data.computerName) and any arrays require mv-expand.

SentinelOneAlert.description: SentinelOne Singularity / Unified Alert collected by Ingext from the SentinelOne alerts API. Each record is one normalized alert raised by a SentinelOne product (EDR, Cloud, Identity, STAR, etc.): the detection (name/description, classification, severity, confidence, verdict, and mitigation result), the affected asset, the triggering process and its file, and the detection source. This is SentinelOne's newer normalized alert schema and is distinct from the legacy SentinelOneThreat resource — an alert references its underlying threat via externalId and shares correlation context through storylineId. Nested objects (asset, process, detectionSource) are dynamic and accessed with dot notation.

SentinelOneThreat.description: SentinelOne threat/detection resource snapshot collected by Ingext from the SentinelOne management API (threats). WindowsAudit.description:
Windows audit events collected from the Windows Security event log (and a few adjacent channels) and forwarded by NXLog's im_msvistalog module as JSON. Like the Office365 audit stream, this is one wide, sparse schema: every record carries a common NXLog/Windows envelope (EventID, EventTime, Hostname, Channel, EventType, ...), and the numeric EventID selects which additional fields are present. Use the per-field 'applicableEventIDs' list to know whether a field is populated for the event you are querying, and always constrain on EventID first — a query that filters on TargetUserName without pinning EventID will mix logons, group changes and Kerberos ticket requests into one result set.
The record is stored as a dynamic JSON document, so any field can be referenced directly by name. Two typing rules matter when writing KQL:
  * Fields from the event's <System> block (EventID, Task, Version, ProcessID,
    ThreadID, RecordNumber, Keywords, OpcodeValue, SeverityValue) arrive as
    JSON numbers.
  * Fields from the event's <EventData> block arrive as strings, even when
    they look numeric — LogonType is "3", KeyLength is "0", IpPort is "0",
    SubjectLogonId is "0x0". Compare them as strings, or wrap in toint()/
    tolong() first. Hex values (LogonId, Status, TicketOptions, AccessMask)
    are lowercase "0x"-prefixed strings and should be compared as strings.

Several EventData fields carry Windows message-table references rather than text — a "%%NNNN" token (for example ElevatedToken "%%1842" = Yes). The common tokens are documented on the individual fields below.

ZPAUserActivity.description: Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) user activity log, streamed by Ingext from a ZPA Log Streaming Service (LSS) user-activity feed (log type zpn_trans_log). Each record is one application connection brokered by ZPA: the user and client device (identity, platform, private/public IP, geolocation), the application and app group requested, the App Connector and server that fulfilled the request, the access-policy rule that matched, connection status and byte counts through the ZPA Service Edge (ZEN), a detailed timeline of setup timestamps, and Privileged Remote Access (PRA) session details when applicable. Field semantics follow the Zscaler "User Activity Log Fields" specification for LSS JSON feeds. Unlike the ZIA NSS feeds, numeric fields arrive as native JSON numbers. timestamp is parsed from the 'LogTimestamp' field. Timing fields (PolicyProcessingTime, ServerSetupTime) are in microseconds.

ZscalerDNS.description: Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) DNS control log, streamed by Ingext from a Zscaler NSS DNS-log feed. Each record is one DNS request/response the Zscaler cloud firewall's DNS control processed: who/where (user, department, location, client device), the query (name and record type) and answer, the client source and Zscaler server destination addresses, the DNS category, and the policy actions and matched rules applied separately to the request and the response. Field semantics follow the Zscaler "NSS Feed Output Format: DNS Logs" specification. The NSS feed parser parses srv_dport and durationms as numbers. timestamp is parsed from the 'datetime' field.

ZscalerFirewall.description: Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) cloud firewall session log, streamed by Ingext from a Zscaler NSS firewall-log feed. Each record is one network session (or an aggregate of sessions) the Zscaler cloud firewall processed: who/where (user, department, location, client device, tunnel), the full client/server address pairs across NAT (client source/dest and server source/dest IP:port), the firewall verdict and matched rule, the network service/application, byte counts and durations, and security context (IP category, threat, destination country). Field semantics follow the Zscaler "NSS Feed Output Format: Firewall Logs" specification. The NSS feed parser parses the numeric fields (csport, cdport, ssport, sdport, tunsport, numsessions, inbytes, outbytes, duration, durationms, avgduration) as numbers. timestamp is parsed from the 'datetime' field.

ZscalerWeb.description: Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) web proxy transaction log, streamed by Ingext from a Zscaler NSS (Nanolog Streaming Service) web-log feed. Each record is one HTTP/HTTPS transaction a user's device made through the Zscaler cloud proxy: who/where (login, department, location, client device), the request (URL, host, method, user-agent), the proxy verdict (action, applied rule), the response (status code, sizes, timing), and security/classification context (URL category class, cloud-app name/class, malware/threat, DLP, risk score). Field semantics follow the Zscaler "NSS Feed Output Format: Web Logs" specification. The NSS feed parser parses the numeric fields (reqsize, respsize, respcode, riskscore, ctime, stime) as numbers. timestamp is parsed from the 'time' field.

msDefenderAvHealth.description:
Microsoft Defender Antivirus health and configuration state per device, collected by Ingext from the Defender for Endpoint API (GET /api/deviceavinfo — the "device health and antivirus compliance" report). Each record is the current AV posture of one device: the mode Defender Antivirus is running in (active / passive / disabled / EDR-blocked), the three component versions (security intelligence "signature", engine, platform) with an up-to-date verdict for each, and the outcome and time of the last quick and full scans.
This is the answer to "is Microsoft Defender Antivirus actually protecting this device, and is it current?" — a question msDefenderMachine cannot answer: healthStatus there describes the *EDR sensor*, not the antivirus. A device can be healthStatus Active and still have AV disabled or three weeks of stale signatures.
One row per device (per unique combination of device, AV mode, up-to-date status and scan results, which in practice is one row per device). It is a resource stream: _key is machineId, the resource watch upserts on it, and each _key holds the latest snapshot — no arg_max/dedup pattern is needed. The whole set is re-dumped every 8 hours.
Join to msDefenderMachine on machineId == msDefenderMachine.id for OS, device group, risk and exposure. Two typing traps: the boolean-looking up-to-date fields are *strings* ("True"/"False"/"Unknown"), and avMode is a *string-typed integer* ("0".."5"), so both need string comparison, and avMode needs a case() mapping to be readable.

msDefenderMachine.description:
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) device inventory snapshot, collected by Ingext from the Defender for Endpoint API (GET /api/machines). Each record is the current state of one onboarded device: identity (MDE device id, FQDN, Entra device id), operating system and build, every network interface the sensor reported, onboarding and sensor health, the management channel (Intune / Configuration Manager / MDE), the device group used for RBAC, and the two Defender Vulnerability Management ratings — riskScore (active threat activity) and exposureLevel (vulnerability/misconfiguration exposure).
This is a *resource* stream, not an event stream. It is the Defender for Endpoint API surface (api.security.microsoft.com/api), which is a different API from the Microsoft Graph security API behind MSDefenderAlert / MSDefenderIncident — different host, different token audience, different record shapes. The two must not be confused, but they join: msDefenderMachine.id is the same MDE device id that appears in MSDefenderAlert evidence as evidence[].mdeDeviceId (on '#microsoft.graph.security.deviceEvidence' elements).
Because it is a resource, each device appears exactly once with its latest state: _key is the device id and the resource watch upserts on it. No arg_max/dedup pattern is needed here — unlike MSDefenderAlert and MSDefenderIncident, which are append-only snapshot streams. The whole inventory is re-dumped every 8 hours (with jitter), so a snapshot is at most a few hours stale.
This is the anchor table of the Defender for Endpoint resource family. It joins to msDefenderAvHealth on machineId, to msDefenderSecureConfig on deviceId, and to msDefenderVulnerability on DeviceId — all of them carrying the same device id string. Those three are per-device *finding* tables (one row per device+item), so the join direction is normally: filter here, then look up findings there.
The record is stored as a dynamic JSON document. ipAddresses is an array of objects and needs mv-expand (or mv-apply) to enumerate; machineTags is an array of strings; vmMetadata is an object present only on cloud VMs. timestamp is parsed from lastSeen.

msDefenderRecommendation.description:
Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management security recommendations, collected by Ingext from the Defender for Endpoint API (GET /api/recommendations). Each record is one tenant-wide recommendation — "update this product to version X" or "turn on this hardening control" — with the fleet-wide counts behind it (how many devices are exposed, how many are covered), its weight on the secure score and on exposure, and the threat context that makes it urgent (public exploit, active alert, associated threat campaigns).
This is the *rollup* table of the Defender for Endpoint resource family, and the one to start from for "what should we fix first". The per-device evidence behind each recommendation lives in the other two:

  - id starting 'va-_-' — a software-update recommendation. Its device-level
    findings are msDefenderVulnerability rows whose RecommendationReference
    equals this id.
  - id starting 'sca-_-scid-' — a secure-configuration recommendation. Its
    device-level findings are msDefenderSecureConfig rows whose
    recommendationReference equals this id.

There is no device information in this record at all — only counts — so any question of the form "which devices" requires the join.
It is a resource stream: _key is the recommendation id, the resource watch upserts on it, and each _key holds the latest snapshot, so no arg_max/dedup pattern is needed. The whole set is re-dumped every 8 hours.
ONE TRAP: this endpoint returns no per-record time of any kind, so timestamp is the collection (dump) time, identical across every record in a snapshot. It says when Ingext fetched the recommendation, not when the recommendation appeared or last changed, and it cannot be used to find new or newly-worsened recommendations — compare snapshots for that. It is still the right column for range filters; just keep the window wide enough (>= 1d) to include a dump.
Note also that both scoring fields are populated per record but only one is meaningful per kind: 'va-_-' records carry exposureImpact with configScoreImpact 0, and 'sca-_-scid-' records carry configScoreImpact. Rank within a kind, not across the two.

msDefenderSecureConfig.description:
Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management secure-configuration assessment, per device, collected by Ingext from the Defender for Endpoint API (GET /api/machines/SecureConfigurationsAssessmentByMachine). Each record is one security configuration evaluated on one device — "is this hardening control applicable here, and is it configured correctly?" — so the table is one row per (deviceId, configurationId): a fleet of N devices against M applicable controls produces on the order of N x M rows, typically the second-largest resource in this family after msDefenderVulnerability.
These are the misconfiguration findings behind the Microsoft Secure Score for Devices and the 'Security controls' half of msDefenderRecommendation: each record's recommendationReference ('sca-_-scid-NNN') is the tenant-wide recommendation this device-level finding rolls up into, and configurationImpact is that control's weight in the score.
It is a resource stream: _key is the composite deviceId_configurationId, the resource watch upserts on it, and each _key holds the latest snapshot — no arg_max/dedup pattern is needed. The composite key matters: keying on the device alone would collapse every finding on a device into one.
Three things to get right before counting anything. (1) isApplicable gates everything — a control that does not apply to the platform is reported with isCompliant false, so a non-compliance count that does not filter isApplicable == true is wrong, usually by a lot. (2) timestamp comes from the record's own 'timestamp' field, which the API returns in a space-separated, zone-less UTC form ("2026-07-30 10:32:16"), not RFC3339 — todatetime() parses it, but string comparison against an RFC3339 literal will not match. (3) The device-side field names are camelCase here (deviceId, osPlatform), unlike msDefenderVulnerability, whose export shape is PascalCase.
Join to msDefenderMachine on deviceId == msDefenderMachine.id for device group, exposure and risk, and to msDefenderRecommendation on recommendationReference == msDefenderRecommendation.id to get the tenant-wide view of the same control.

msDefenderSecureScore.description:
Microsoft Secure Score for Devices — the organization-wide device hardening score — collected by Ingext from the Defender for Endpoint API (GET /api/configurationScore). A higher score means the endpoint estate is more resilient; the score rises as the secure-configuration recommendations in msDefenderRecommendation are applied.
THIS TABLE HOLDS EXACTLY ONE RECORD. The endpoint returns a single entity rather than a collection, and because the record has no natural key the resource watch keys it on the literal resource name, so every 8-hour cycle overwrites the one row in place. Consequences, in order of how often they trip a query up:

  - No history. The table cannot be trended, differenced, or charted over time —
    it always holds the current score and nothing else. 'summarize by bin(time,
    1d)' returns one bucket. To trend the score, snapshot this row into another
    table on a schedule, or reconstruct the trend from the recommendation
    backlog instead.
  - No grouping. Every aggregation over a one-row table is that row. Just
    project it, or use toscalar() to pull the score into another query — see
    queries/mde-secure-score-headroom.yaml.
  - A stale row is possible. If a cycle fails to fetch the score (the resource
    needs its own Score.Read.All permission), the previous row stays in place
    unchanged. Always report the record's own 'time' alongside the score rather
    than assuming it is current.

The score is a raw point total, not a percentage: the API returns no maximum, so the percentage the Defender portal displays cannot be derived from this record alone. The achievable headroom is available though — sum configScoreImpact over the active 'sca-_-scid-' recommendations in msDefenderRecommendation, whose per-device evidence is msDefenderSecureConfig. Those three tables and this one describe the same thing at three levels of detail: the fleet score here, the per-control rollup there, and the per-device findings in msDefenderSecureConfig.
Note that this is the *device* secure score (Defender Vulnerability Management, driven by endpoint configuration), which is a different measure from the tenant-wide Microsoft Secure Score in the Defender portal that also covers identity and apps. The two are not comparable and do not share a scale.

msDefenderVulnerability.description:
Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management software-vulnerability assessment, per device, collected by Ingext from the Defender for Endpoint API. Each record is one CVE affecting one software product on one device, so the table is one row per (device, software vendor, software name, software version, CVE) — by far the largest resource in this family: a mid-size tenant produces millions of rows, and a single device commonly carries hundreds.
It answers "which devices are exposed to this CVE, and what update fixes it?" Alongside it, msDefenderSecureConfig covers the misconfiguration half of the same exposure picture, and msDefenderRecommendation is the tenant-wide rollup of both.
It is a resource stream: _key is the record Id, the resource watch upserts on it, and each _key holds the latest snapshot — no arg_max/dedup pattern is needed. The snapshot has no history: a CVE that gets patched simply stops appearing, so "when was this fixed" cannot be answered from this table (compare FirstSeenTimestamp against an older report instead).
FIELD NAME CASING — the one trap that breaks queries outright. The connector can fetch this data from three sources (set per integration by 'vulnerabilitySource'), and they do not agree on field names or on the record width:

  - files (default) and export — the TVM export shapes. Wide record, PascalCase
    names (DeviceId, CveId, CvssScore, LastSeenTimestamp), device named
    DeviceId. This is the shape documented field-by-field below and shown in
    eventSamples/msDefenderVulnerability_export.json.
  - odata — the legacy /api/vulnerabilities/machinesVulnerabilities collection.
    A compact camelCase record (id, cveId, machineId, fixingKbId, productName,
    productVendor, productVersion, severity) that names the device machineId,
    not deviceId, and carries none of the OS, CVSS, exploitability, timestamp
    or recommendation fields.

Field names are matched case-sensitively, so a query written against one shape returns nothing at all against the other. Confirm which source a tenant uses before writing against it; if a query must survive either, coalesce the pairs (e.g. coalesce(DeviceId, machineId), coalesce(CveId, cveId)). Switching sources also changes the Id values themselves, which retires the old resource keys and creates a new set.
Timestamps here are the space-separated, zone-less UTC form ("2026-07-30 10:32:16"), not RFC3339 — todatetime() parses it, but comparing the raw string against an RFC3339 literal will not match.

sentinelOneAgent.description: SentinelOne endpoint agent resource snapshot collected by Ingext from the SentinelOne management API (agents inventory). Each record is the current state of one installed agent/endpoint: hardware and OS, agent version and health, protection/mitigation posture, scan and threat status, network/management connectivity, site/group placement, and last logged-in user. The object is stored as a dynamic JSON document, so nested objects are accessed with dot notation (e.g. activeDirectory.computerDistinguishedName) and arrays require mv-expand.

sentinelOneApplication.description: SentinelOne application-inventory resource snapshot collected by Ingext from the SentinelOne management API (installed applications). Each record is one application installed on one endpoint: application identity (name, version, publisher, signed/risk), install/update timestamps, size, and a denormalized set of agent.* fields identifying the endpoint it is installed on. Because each row is per (agent, application), the same application appears once per endpoint it is installed on. The object is stored as a dynamic JSON document; use mv-expand for any nested arrays.
